title: Senior's toolkit: async in production
summary: Cancellation, timeouts, HttpClient done right, and the tools for diagnosing a hung or starved service.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: async in production
steps.body: Async bugs show up under load: requests that hang, a thread pool that runs dry, calls that never time out. These are the APIs that prevent them and the tools for finding them in a running process.

toolkit.what: Accept a token in every async method and pass it to every async call inside. In ASP.NET Core, an endpoint's `CancellationToken` parameter is cancelled when the client disconnects.
flags: a token that cancels itself after a timeout
combine the caller's token with your own timeout
check inside a long CPU loop
toolkit.example:
app.MapGet("/report", async (ReportService svc, CancellationToken ct) =>
    Results.Ok(await svc.BuildAsync(ct)));

toolkit.what: Start independent calls together and wait for all of them. The results come back in the same order as the tasks, whatever finishes first.
flags: only the first exception; look at `whenAll.Exception.InnerExceptions` for all
the first one to finish, e.g. for a race against a fallback

toolkit.what: Stop waiting for a task after a timeout (throws `TimeoutException`) or when a token is cancelled. The task itself keeps running, so prefer passing a token to the call when you can.
flags: what you catch when time is up

toolkit.what: Let `IHttpClientFactory` create and recycle `HttpClient` handlers, so you avoid both socket exhaustion (a new HttpClient per call) and stale DNS (one forever). Add timeouts and retries with the Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience package.
flags: a class that takes `HttpClient` in its constructor
timeouts, retries with backoff and a circuit breaker

toolkit.what: Watch a running .NET process's live metrics: CPU, GC, exceptions per second, and the thread pool. Install once with `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-counters`.
flags: the runtime counters, including thread pool queue length and thread count
list the .NET processes you can attach to
toolkit.when: the service is slow or hangs under load and you need to see why

toolkit.what: Print the managed call stack of every thread in a running process. When 200 threads all sit in `Task.Result` or `.Wait()`, you have found the sync-over-async call.
toolkit.when: a hang in an environment where you cannot attach a debugger

toolkit.what: Visual Studio's debugger views of every thread and every async task at once, grouped by identical stacks. A deadlock or a pile-up of awaiting tasks is visible at a glance.
flags: threads or tasks as a merged graph
each task, its status and what it is awaiting
toolkit.example: Break All, Debug > Windows > Parallel Stacks, switch the view to Tasks

steps.prompt: Under load the API stops answering. `dotnet-counters` shows the thread pool queue length climbing past 2,000 and the thread count rising slowly, while CPU stays at 5%. `dotnet-stack report` shows hundreds of threads waiting in `Task.Result`. What is the cause?
options: Sync-over-async: code blocks a thread with `.Result` on an async call, so the thread pool starves; make the call chain `await` all the way up
The server needs more CPU cores
The garbage collector is running too often
steps.explain: Low CPU, a growing queue and blocked threads are the classic starvation picture. Every blocked thread waits for work that needs another thread to run; the pool only adds threads slowly. The fix is `await`, not a bigger pool.

code: async Task<int> Work(int ms, int value) { await Task.Delay(ms); return value; }
var results = await Task.WhenAll(Work(30, 1), Work(10, 2), Work(20, 3));
steps.explain: `WhenAll` returns results in the order the tasks were passed, not the order they finished. A cancelled token makes `Delay` throw `TaskCanceledException`, which is an `OperationCanceledException`.

steps.prompt: Match each tool or API to its job.
pairs: watch thread pool queue length live
dump every thread's stack from a running process
stop waiting for a slow task
combine the caller's cancellation with your own timeout

steps.prompt: Give the call 5 seconds, but also stop if the request is aborted.
steps.explain: The linked source cancels when either the request's token or the timer fires. Pass `cts.Token`, and dispose the source (`using`) so its timer is released.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Every async method takes a `CancellationToken` and passes it on, and every outgoing call has a timeout. Never block on `.Result` or `.Wait()` in server code. When a service hangs, look before you guess: `dotnet-counters` for the thread pool, `dotnet-stack` or Parallel Stacks for where the threads are stuck.
